It works by sensing the current temperature and comparing it to a setpoint, or desired temperature, that you choose. When the temperature deviates from the setpoint, the thermostat sends signals to your heating or cooling system to turn on or off, maintaining the desired temperature. How does a thermostat control temperature? Thermostats work by using a temperature sensor, often a bimetallic strip or a digital thermistor, to detect the room’s temperature. This sensor sends information to the thermostat’s control system, which compares it to your set temperature. If the room is colder than the setpoint, the thermostat signals the heating system to turn on. Conversely, if the room is warmer, it signals the cooling system to activate. This continuous cycle of sensing and adjusting maintains the desired temperature. Why should I use a programmable thermostat? Programmable thermostats offer significant benefits, primarily energy savings. By setting different temperatures for different times of day, you can optimize your heating and cooling usage. Why does the heating system keep running after reaching the set temperature? Heat already stored in the furnace, ducts, radiators, or room surfaces can keep raising the air temperature after the call for heat ends. Some equipment also has a short fan or shutdown delay; a system that runs continuously well past the set point needs troubleshooting. Does a thermostat switch on at exactly the displayed temperature? Usually, no. The control uses a small range around the set point to prevent rapid on-off cycling, so heating may start below the displayed setting and stop after the room warms through it. passages.text: A thermostat is a crucial device in maintaining a comfortable and stable indoor environment. It regulates the temperature by controlling the heating or cooling system. The main components of a thermostat include the sensing element, control unit, and actuator. The sensing element, typically a thermistor or thermometer, monitors the temperature of the room. The control unit, which is the brain of the thermostat, processes the temperature data and sends signals to the actuator. The actuator, usually a motor or relay, turns the heating or cooling system on or off to maintain the desired temperature. The sensing element is responsible for detecting the temperature of the room. Thermistors are commonly used in thermostats due to their high accuracy and fast response time. They consist of a small piece of semiconductor material that changes its resistance in response to temperature changes. Thermometers, on the other hand, measure temperature using a liquid or gas that expands or contracts in response to temperature changes. You might have a temperature control on a wall in your home to control the heating system but, although it's probably marked in degrees, it's not a thermometer. It's called a thermostat, a modern word based on two ancient Greek ones: thermo (meaning heat) and statos (which means standing and is related to words like stasis, status quo, and static—meaning to stay the same). We can tell just from its name that a thermostat is something that "keeps heat the same": when our home is too cold, the thermostat switches on the heating so things quickly warm up; once the temperature reaches the level we've set, the thermostat switches the heating off so we don't boil. Let's just be clear about the difference: a thermometer is something that measures the temperature; a thermostat is something that tries to maintain the temperature (keep it roughly the same). passages.text: Why Heating And Cooling Cycle Differently A thermostat usually doesn’t switch on at exactly the displayed temperature; it uses a control range around the set point, and heating and cooling respond on opposite sides of that range. Set heating to 68°F, for example, and the system may start after the sensor falls below the target and stop once the sensor reaches its heating control range. A 68°F Heating Setting The displayed 68°F is a target, not a magic instant. The thermostat starts a heating call after the sensed air drops far enough below its control range, then ends the call as the sensor rises through that range. The exact start and stop points depend on the control and equipment. Heat can continue moving after the thermostat ends the call. A furnace blower may clear stored heat from the heat exchanger, a hydronic circulator may move hot water already in the pipes, and a heat-pump fan may follow a control-board delay or a defrost and protection routine. Brief run-on can be normal. Cooling calls begin when room temperature rises above the cooling range, then the air conditioner may wait through a compressor anti-short-cycle delay before restarting. passages.text: How Thermostats Control Temperature in Your Home On this page 7 sections A temperature control thermostat regulates indoor climate by sensing temperature changes and adjusting heating or cooling systems to maintain the desired setting. Thermostats are the brains behind your home’s heating and cooling systems. These clever devices constantly monitor indoor temperatures and activate your HVAC equipment to maintain your desired comfort level. From simple mechanical switches to advanced smart systems, thermostats have evolved significantly while maintaining the same core function: keeping your home at the perfect temperature. How Thermostats Work: The Basic Principle All thermostats operate on the same fundamental principle – they act as switches that turn your heating or cooling system on and off based on temperature readings. When the room temperature drops below your set point, the thermostat activates the heater. When temperatures rise above the setting, it turns on the air conditioner or shuts off the heat. Mechanical vs. Digital Thermostats Traditional mechanical thermostats use bimetallic strips that bend with temperature changes to physically open or close electrical circuits.
